To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) OpenStack is the only virtualization technology that is able to support the chaining of virtual network functions; 2) Open vSwitch is the virtual switch that can support the chaining of network functions in OpenStack; and 3) the performance of the virtualization technologies is affected by the type of traffic and by the number of virtual network functions.
the virtualization technologies (VMs, VNFs) are not suitable to run the virtual network functions (VNFs) in NFV.

1) Open vSwitch is the most suitable technology to implement virtualized switches in NFV; 2) OpenStack is the most suitable platform to implement virtualized network functions in NFV; and 3) KVM is the most suitable virtualization platform for virtualized network functions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the assessment of virtual network functions performance, when running on top of virtualization technologies.

the performance assessment of the most popular virtualization technologies (i.e., KVM, Xen, and VMware) when running the most common virtual network functions (i.e., Open vSwitch and OpenDayLight) in order to create a complex service (i.e., a virtual router).
the performance of virtualization technologies in a NFV scenario, where the virtualized network functions are deployed in virtual machines and chained in order to provide a service to a client.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the performance of virtualization technologies for NFV is still far away to be satisfactory.
, although the virtualization technologies can be exploited in NFV, their performances are far from the ones expected by the network operators.
, for the moment, the virtualization technologies that are used for NFV are not able to fully support the requirements of the NFV paradigm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
virtualization technologies perform differently when used in a network scenario than in a cloud computing environment.
virtual machines and containers have comparable performance, and they outperform the hypervisor-based virtualization.
the virtualization technologies are able to support NFV with good performances, but they are not able to provide the same performance levels as the dedicated appliances.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the performance of the virtualization technologies in a NFV scenario is significantly different from the performance in the cloud computing scenario, which means that a different benchmarking is required.
the performance of virtualization technologies is highly affected by the traffic they process.
the virtualization technologies that have been developed to support cloud computing, can be used to implement NFV as well, but their performances are not the same in both contexts.
